To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the bacterial L11 is able to replace its yeast orthologue, although the bacterial protein does not restore the correct acidic protein composition of the yeast ribosome, and, moreover the ribosome containing bacterial L11 becomes sensitive to the proaryotic specific antibiotic, thiostrepton.

1) the assembly of bacterial L12 in yeast ribosomes restores their polymerase activity and 2) the assembly of L11 from E. coli in yeast ribosomes confers partial sensitivity to the prokayotic antibiotic thiostrepon.
the assembly of a prokaryotic ribosomal protein into the yeast ribosomal particles induces the formation of a ribosome structure that is partially sensitive to a prokaryote specific antibiotic.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the assembly of a prokaryotic ribosomal protein into a eukaryotic ribosome and the consequences of this process in the structure and function of the ribosome.
the assembly of a prokaryotic ribosomal protein into eukaryotic ribosomes and its effect on the ribosomal function.
the in vivo assembly of the bacterial protein L11 into the eukaryotic ribosome.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the bacterial protein is not a good substitute for yeast ScL12 in vivo.
the bacterial protein L11, although correctly incorporated into yeast ribosomes, does not fully replace its eukaryotic counterpart in the ribosomal structure and functions.
the yeast ribosomes containing EcL11 have a higher affinity for the antibiotic, although the growth of the yeast strain is not affected.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
EcL11 is able to partially replace ScL12 in yeast ribosomes but the assembly of the bacterial protein in the eukaryotic ribosome is not perfect and it induces a partial loss of ribosomal function.
the bacterial protein L11 is able to assemble in the yeast ribosomal particle, but it is unable to substitute for the yeast L12 protein, at least in vivo.
the assembly of the bacterial protein into the yeast ribosomes is correct, but the ribosomes are unable to perform the same functions of the bacterial ones.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, despite the structural and functional differences between eukaryotic L12 and bacterial L11, the latter is able to assemble into yeast ribosomes and partially restore the growth rate of L12-defective cells.

the assembly of bacterial L12 into the yeast ribosomal stalk does not restore the correct protein composition and that the assembly of L11 in the yeast ribosomal body does not restore the full function of the protein.
the bacterial L11 can be correctly assembled into yeast ribosomes and that the CTD of L11 is involved in the interaction with thiostrepton.
